findings.claim: The `put` arm of handle_request calls three `unwrap()`s on untrusted wire input, so a malformed request panics and terminates the process instead of returning Response::Error. `parts.next().unwrap()` panics when the request has no key segment ("put"), the second `parts.next().unwrap()` panics when there is no ttl segment ("put:k"), and `.parse().unwrap()` panics when the ttl segment is not a valid u64 ("put:k:abc", "put:k:-1"). The sibling `get` arm shows the intended pattern: a missing segment yields Response::Error("bad request").
findings.proposedReproduction: Reachable end-to-end from kvstore-cli/src/main.rs:9, which forwards raw argv into handle_request: `kvstore-cli put` -> panic at api.rs:26 (unwrap on None); `kvstore-cli put:k` -> panic at api.rs:27 (unwrap on None); `kvstore-cli put:k:abc` -> panic at api.rs:27 (unwrap on ParseIntError). Library-level: handle_request(&mut Cache::new(64), "put:k") panics.

findings.claim: SharedCounter::read_or_init acquires the mutex three separate times instead of once, so the check and the read are not atomic. Between `self.inner.lock().unwrap().contains_key(key)` returning true on line 77 and `self.inner.lock().unwrap().get(key).unwrap()` on line 78, the lock is released; a concurrent `remove(key)` deletes the entry, `get` then returns None, and `.unwrap()` panics. The whole check-then-act sequence must hold one guard across both operations.
findings.proposedReproduction: Let c: Arc<SharedCounter> already contain key "k". Interleaving: T1 executes line 77, locks, contains_key("k") -> true, drops the temporary guard at the end of the statement. T2 calls c.remove("k"), which locks and removes "k". T1 resumes at line 78, locks, get("k") -> None, unwrap() panics. The panic also poisons the mutex, so every subsequent lock().unwrap() in read_or_init and remove panics too.

findings.claim: evict_oldest evicts n+1 entries rather than the n its doc comment promises, because the loop uses the inclusive range `for _ in 0..=n` instead of `0..n`. Since Cache::put calls evict_oldest(overflow + 1) with overflow == 0 in the ordinary full-cache case, every write to a full cache drops two entries when exactly one needed to go, so the cache silently loses live entries and steady-state occupancy falls below max_entries.
findings.proposedReproduction:
let mut c = Cache::new(4); c.put("a","1"); c.put("b","2"); c.put("c","3"); c.put("d","4"); // len == 4 == max
c.put("e","5"); // len 4 >= 4 -> overflow = 0 -> evict_oldest(1) -> loop runs twice, popping "a" and "b"
assert_eq!(c.len(), 4) FAILS: c.len() == 3, and c.get("b") == None even though evicting "a" alone would have satisfied the bound. Directly: c.evict_oldest(1) on a 4-entry cache leaves 2 entries, not 3.

findings.claim: Cache::put does not special-case overwriting an existing key. It triggers eviction whenever `map.len() >= max_entries` even though re-inserting a present key does not grow the map, and it unconditionally pushes the key onto `order` again. Consequently an update to an already-cached key evicts unrelated live entries that were within the bound, and `order` accumulates duplicate keys so it desynchronizes from `map` — a later pop_front can remove a key that was just re-written, or be a no-op on an already-removed key that fails to free the slot it was called to free.
